sections.overview: This North American hare inhabits boreal and mountain forests, from Alaska and Newfoundland south to the western mountains and Appalachians. Its name recalls broad, furred hind feet that aid travel over soft snow. Herbivorous, it also feeds many mammalian and bird predators, so its abundance affects other populations. Northern numbers cycle strongly, while many southern populations fluctuate less.
sections.identification: Adults average 46–51 centimetres and 1.4–1.8 kilograms in Alaska; size varies regionally, so these are indicative figures. The coat usually changes from brown or grey-brown in summer to white in winter, with dark ear tips and a small tail. Large, furred hind feet spread weight over snow and reduce sinking. On coastal parts of British Columbia, Washington and Oregon, where snow is scarce, hares may remain brown year-round. Females are often slightly larger than males.
sections.habitat: Across most of its range, the hare favors boreal or upper-montane forest with dense understory, where shrubs provide food and concealment. In California it also uses dense conifer stands, high-elevation riparian woods and chaparral. It rests in a shallow ground hollow called a form, often beneath brush, ferns or fallen timber, rather than digging a burrow. Well-used runways connect feeding patches and shelter; snow makes them conspicuous and can preserve summer routes.
sections.diet: In California, grasses, forbs and succulent plants are important summer foods; in snowy winters, hares there rely mainly on conifer needles and evergreen shrub leaves. Newfoundland menus include birch, willow, maple, balsam fir, grasses and fireweed, illustrating regional variation. Like other lagomorphs, hares re-ingest soft nutrient-rich droppings called cecotropes, passing food through the gut again so more nutrients can be absorbed. This helps recover nutrients from fibrous plants, while nutritious young growth remains valuable when available.
sections.behavior: Snowshoe hares are generally solitary outside breeding, although overlapping home ranges and temporary feeding aggregations occur. They are active mainly at dusk and night, resting by day in sheltered cover. Individuals communicate partly by thumping their hind feet, a reported warning or contact signal, and may squeal when captured. Females and males may each have several mates; this does not make hares a stable social group.
sections.reproduction: Breeding dates vary with latitude and local conditions; in many northern populations, mating begins in late winter or spring and continues into summer. Gestation lasts about 36–37 days; litters range from one to six leverets and average three, with counts varying locally. A female may conceive again before her previous litter is born, allowing several litters in a long season. Leverets are born fully furred, open-eyed and mobile; they nurse once daily and become self-supporting at three to four weeks.
sections.ecology: Lynx, coyotes and foxes hunt snowshoe hares, as do numerous hawks and owls; no single predator explains every local trend. Yukon field experiments found that reducing mammalian predation and adding food each raised hare density, while doing both had a larger combined effect. Predator numbers often follow hare abundance with a delay, and may shift to other prey when hares become scarce. At population peaks, browsing can reduce young shoots, linking plant availability with predation.
sections.conservation: The species is widespread and classified as Secure in Canada in the 2020 General Status assessment, a national screening rather than legal protection. In California, where it occupies a limited set of high-elevation regions, the wildlife agency lists it as a Species of Special Concern. In Alaska, the wildlife agency lists development, mining and fuel exploration as habitat threats. Shorter snow seasons can leave winter-white hares conspicuous against bare ground. Montana research found mismatches during spring and autumn molts; spring color change can respond to snow conditions, but does not track every local change perfectly.
